topics.name: Oracy and Presentation
objectives: Give well-structured descriptions, explanations and narratives for different purposes
Use spoken language to develop understanding through speculating, hypothesising, imagining and exploring ideas
Participate in discussions, presentations, performances, role play and debates
Gain, maintain and monitor the interest of the listener
Select and use appropriate registers for effective communication

keyVocab.definition: The style and formality of language chosen to suit the audience and purpose
A structured argument where speakers take opposing views
A tentative idea or explanation to be explored
Language used to persuade or influence an audience
The feeling or attitude conveyed through the voice or writing

masteryIndicators: I can adapt my language for different audiences and purposes
I can present an argument clearly with supporting evidence
I can use persuasive techniques when speaking
I can listen critically and respond with a counter-argument
topics.starter: Hot Seat: one pupil in role as a book character — class asks questions to find out more
topics.guidedPractice: Structured debate: teacher models 'I agree/disagree because…'; class practises formal opening statements
topics.independentPractice: Developing: use sentence stems (I think… because…). Expected: present a structured argument. Mastery: formal debate with rebuttal.
topics.masteryCheck: Give a 1-minute talk on a given topic. Assess: vocabulary, structure, engagement of audience.

topics.name: Word Reading and Vocabulary
objectives: Apply growing knowledge of root words, prefixes and suffixes to read aloud and understand the meaning of unfamiliar words
Read further exception words, noting unusual correspondences between spelling and pronunciation
Identify/explain the meaning of words in context
Discuss, explore and investigate word meanings, origins and associations

keyVocab.definition: The base form of a word before any prefixes or suffixes are added
The origin and history of a word
The surrounding text that helps you work out the meaning of a word
The feeling or associations a word suggests beyond its literal meaning
A word with a similar meaning
A word with an opposite meaning

masteryIndicators: I can work out the meaning of an unfamiliar word using roots and context
I can explain the effect of a word choice in a text
I can discuss synonyms and antonyms and explain differences in connotation
I can explain the origin of a word
topics.starter: Word detectives: given 3 words with the same root — what do they share?
topics.guidedPractice: Read a passage together: pause on 3 words — model using context and root knowledge to infer meaning
topics.independentPractice: Developing: use a glossary to find word meanings. Expected: use context to infer meaning. Mastery: explore connotations and word choice effect.
topics.masteryCheck: Explain the meaning of [word] as used in the text. Why has the author chosen this word?

topics.name: Reading for Meaning
objectives: Develop positive attitudes to reading and understanding of what they read
Identify themes and conventions in a wide range of books
Make inferences from what is stated and implied
Identify how language, structure and presentation contribute to meaning
Retrieve and record information from non-fiction

keyVocab.definition: A big idea that runs through a text, e.g. friendship, courage
Working out what the author means from clues in the text
Find information that is directly stated in the text
How a text is organised — paragraphs, sections, chapters
Reading quickly to get the gist or find a specific piece of information
Looking through a text to locate a specific word or piece of information

masteryIndicators: I can make inferences and support them with evidence from the text
I can retrieve and record information accurately
I can explain what a theme is and give an example from the text
I can explain how structure helps the reader
topics.starter: Inference warm-up: read 2–3 sentences — what can you infer about the character?
topics.guidedPractice: Shared reading: teacher models finding evidence to support inference using a PEDR frame (Point, Evidence, Develop, Relate)
topics.independentPractice: Developing: retrieval questions. Expected: inference with evidence. Mastery: analyse how structure contributes to meaning.
topics.masteryCheck: Answer: one retrieval, one inference, one theme question — all with text evidence.

topics.name: Critical Reading
objectives: Identify and discuss themes and conventions in a wide range of writing
Make comparisons within and across books
Ask questions to improve their understanding
Infer characters' feelings, thoughts and motives from their actions
Distinguish between statements of fact and opinion
Provide reasoned justifications for their views

keyVocab.definition: A preference for one viewpoint over others, often without fair consideration of alternatives
A point of view or way of seeing something
Suggested or implied but not directly stated
Clearly stated directly in the text
A recurring symbol, image or idea in a text
Identify similarities and differences between two texts or elements

masteryIndicators: I can compare two texts and explain similarities and differences
I can distinguish fact from opinion and explain the difference
I can explain a character's motives using evidence
I can evaluate the effectiveness of an author's choices
topics.starter: Fact or opinion sort: give pupils a mix of statements to categorise
topics.guidedPractice: Compare two newspaper articles on the same event — identify bias, differing viewpoints; model analytical response
topics.independentPractice: Developing: identify one perspective in the text. Expected: compare viewpoints with evidence. Mastery: evaluate and critique authorial intent.
topics.masteryCheck: Is this text biased? Give three pieces of evidence to support your answer.

topics.name: Spelling
objectives: Use further prefixes and suffixes and understand how to add them: -ation, -ly, -ous, -tion, -sion, -cian, -ssion
Place the possessive apostrophe accurately in words with regular plurals
Use the first two or three letters of a word to check its spelling in a dictionary
Apply knowledge of morphology and etymology to spelling
Spell words with 'silent' letters (e.g. knight, psalm, solemn)
Use hyphens to avoid ambiguity
Distinguish between homophones and near-homophones

keyVocab.definition: The study of the structure of words including roots, prefixes and suffixes
An apostrophe (') used to show belonging, e.g. the dog's bone
Words that sound the same but have different spellings and meanings, e.g. there/their/they're
The origin and history of a word
A punctuation mark (-) used to join words or separate syllables

masteryIndicators: I can spell words from the Year 3/4 and Year 5/6 statutory word lists
I can apply morphological rules to spell new words
I can correctly use homophones in context
I can use a dictionary to check spelling and meaning
topics.starter: Homophone challenge: write the correct version of there/their/they're in 5 sentences
topics.guidedPractice: Word investigation: look at the root 'port' — transport, import, export, portable — what do they share?
topics.independentPractice: Developing: practise statutory spelling list words. Expected: apply suffix rules. Mastery: use etymology to explain and spell related words.
topics.masteryCheck: Dictation: teacher reads 5 sentences using the statutory list and target words. Pupils self-correct.

topics.name: Narrative Writing
objectives: Plan writing by discussing the structure, vocabulary and grammar of similar writing
Draft and write by composing and rehearsing sentences orally before writing
Organise paragraphs around a theme
Create settings, characters and plot in narratives
Use a wide range of devices to build cohesion within and across paragraphs
Assess the effectiveness of their own and others' writing, suggesting improvements
Propose changes to vocabulary, grammar and punctuation to enhance effects
Proofread for spelling and punctuation errors

keyVocab.definition: A group of sentences about the same idea, started on a new line
How well a text flows and connects — using pronouns, connectives and vocabulary links
The time and place where a story happens
The mood or feeling created in a text
How an author shows what a character is like through words, actions and thoughts
The perspective from which a story is told (1st or 3rd person)
A feeling of excitement or suspense created to engage the reader

masteryIndicators: I can plan and write a narrative with a clear beginning, middle and end
I can develop a character or setting through word choice
I can use paragraphs to organise my writing
I can edit and improve my own writing for effect
topics.starter: Show an image: pupils write one sentence of description — share; discuss most effective language choices
topics.guidedPractice: Shared writing: co-construct an opening paragraph for a story, teacher thinks aloud about choices; pupils evaluate
topics.independentPractice: Developing: complete a narrative scaffold. Expected: plan and write an opening independently. Mastery: write a complete narrative; experiment with narrative voice and structure for effect.
topics.masteryCheck: Swap writing with a partner — use WAGOLL (What A Good One Looks Like) checklist to give one positive and one target.

topics.name: Persuasive Writing
objectives: Write for a range of real purposes and audiences including persuasion
Use a range of sentence structures for effect
Use modal verbs or adverbs to indicate degrees of possibility
Use devices to build cohesion, including repetition and rhetorical questions
Use the passive voice to affect how information is presented

keyVocab.definition: Writing that aims to change the reader's view or get them to do something
A question asked for effect — not expecting an actual answer
A verb expressing possibility or necessity: can, could, will, would, should, must, might
A sentence structure where the object becomes the subject, e.g. 'Mistakes were made'
The opposing viewpoint — skilled persuasive writers acknowledge and dismiss it
Persuasive techniques: Alliteration, Facts, Opinions, Rhetorical questions, Emotive language, Statistics, Triples

masteryIndicators: I can use rhetorical questions and emotive language for effect
I can structure a persuasive argument using PEEL (Point, Evidence, Explain, Link)
I can use modal verbs to express certainty and possibility
I can include a counter-argument and refute it
topics.starter: Read two adverts — identify persuasive techniques used; rank them by effectiveness
topics.guidedPractice: Model PEEL paragraph together on the board: one persuasive point, with evidence and explanation
topics.independentPractice: Developing: write one persuasive sentence. Expected: write a PEEL paragraph. Mastery: full persuasive text with counter-argument and varied techniques.
topics.masteryCheck: Write a persuasive opening paragraph (5–7 sentences). Identify two techniques you used and explain why.

topics.name: Poetry
objectives: Prepare and perform poems, showing understanding through intonation, tone, volume and action
Discuss and express views about an author's choice of vocabulary
Identify how language, structure and presentation contribute to meaning in poetry
Compose poems drawing on the work of other poets

keyVocab.definition: A group of lines in a poem (like a paragraph in prose)
The beat or pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a poem
The pattern of rhymes at the end of lines, labelled ABAB, AABB, etc.
A comparison using 'like' or 'as'
A comparison that says one thing IS another
Giving human qualities to non-human things
Repeated consonant sounds at the start of nearby words

masteryIndicators: I can identify and explain the effect of a poetic device
I can write a poem using at least two techniques
I can perform a poem with expression and impact
I can compare two poems and discuss similarities and differences
topics.starter: Read a poem aloud twice — first for pleasure, second to identify techniques
topics.guidedPractice: Model writing a stanza inspired by a shared poem: make choices aloud about word sound and rhythm
topics.independentPractice: Developing: complete a poem frame. Expected: write an independent stanza. Mastery: write a complete original poem with deliberate technique choices.
topics.masteryCheck: Write one stanza of a poem. Underline a technique you used. Explain why you chose it.

topics.name: Grammar and Punctuation
objectives: Use fronted adverbials with a comma
Use paragraphs to organise ideas around a theme
Use inverted commas and other punctuation to indicate direct speech
Use and punctuate relative clauses using relative pronouns
Use semi-colons, colons and dashes to mark boundaries between independent clauses
Use a colon to introduce a list
Use bullet points to list information
Use hyphens to avoid ambiguity
Use the subjunctive form in formal writing
Use passive verbs to affect the presentation of information

keyVocab.definition: A word, phrase or clause at the beginning of a sentence telling when, where or how, followed by a comma
A clause that gives more information about a noun, introduced by who, which, that, whose, where, when
Punctuation (;) used to join two closely related independent clauses
Punctuation (:) used to introduce a list or explanation
The actual words spoken by someone, placed inside inverted commas
Additional information added to a sentence, placed in brackets, dashes or commas
A clause that cannot stand alone and depends on the main clause

masteryIndicators: I can use fronted adverbials correctly with a comma
I can punctuate direct speech with inverted commas
I can use relative clauses to add detail
I can use colons and semi-colons to punctuate complex sentences
topics.starter: Fix it: correct the punctuation errors in 3 sentences on the board
topics.guidedPractice: Fronted adverbials: model changing 'She ran quickly' to 'Swiftly, she ran' — discuss effect; class try on whiteboards
topics.independentPractice: Developing: add a fronted adverbial to given sentences. Expected: write sentences using inverted commas and relative clauses. Mastery: rewrite a paragraph using varied, complex sentence structures.
topics.masteryCheck: Write 3 sentences: one with a fronted adverbial, one with a relative clause, one with direct speech.
